scenario.name: Street kiosk — Cola
scenario.description: A street-level kiosk vending machine restocking its single best-seller: Cola. The market price is widely known, the product is a commodity, and the margin is very high. This is the baseline single-item negotiation: volume is the main lever, and the supplier has little room to hide cost.

merchant.name: Budget operator
merchant.description: A high-volume, low-overhead vending operator. Machines are placed in commodity locations (stations, schools). Internal costs are uniformly low because operations are standardised and labour is minimal. Needs deals closed fast — long negotiations waste more money than a bad price.

supplier.name: Local distributor
supplier.description: A regional distributor with its own delivery fleet covering a tight geographic area. Beverage and snack fulfilment is cheap due to bulk routes and proximity. Convenience items are sourced from third parties in small batches, making them expensive to ship. Impatient: a long negotiation ties up a sales rep who could be closing other deals.

history.speaker: MERCHANT
history.content:
Hello, I'm interested in stocking my kiosk. Let's get straight to it. Here is my opening offer:

Cola (330ml): $0.60 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: SUPPLIER
history.content:
Thank you for the offer. However, that price is significantly below the standard wholesale rate for such a popular product. This brand is a consistent top-seller with a strong market price of $1.50.

My offer is:
Cola (330ml): $1.10 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: MERCHANT
history.content:
I understand it's a popular brand, but your price is too close to retail for my business model. A street kiosk relies on volume, and for that to be sustainable, I need a better wholesale price.

I am willing to raise my offer to find a workable middle ground.

My new offer is:
Cola (330ml): $0.80 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: SUPPLIER
history.content:
I appreciate you moving up from your initial offer. However, $0.80 is still not a price point that reflects the value of a premier, high-demand beverage. This product guarantees foot traffic and quick sales, which commands a higher wholesale price.

I can make a small concession to try and close this deal.

My new offer is:
Cola (330ml): $1.00 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: MERCHANT
history.content:
Thank you for moving your price down. I appreciate the flexibility.

While your justification about foot traffic is valid, the final retail price is fixed, and my margins for a high-volume street location are very lean. Your price of $1.00 still doesn't leave enough room. To keep this negotiation moving forward, I am willing to raise my offer again.

My new offer is:
Cola (330ml): $0.90 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: SUPPLIER
history.content:
I understand your position on margins. However, the high volume you anticipate is driven directly by this brand's popularity and consumer willingness to pay the market price. The rapid turnover this product ensures is a significant value in itself.

To demonstrate my commitment to finding a price that works, I'll make one more adjustment. This is the best I can do for a premium, high-velocity product like this.

My new offer is:
Cola (330ml): $0.95 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: MERCHANT
history.content:
We are very close to an agreement. I understand your position on the product's value, and you understand mine on the tight margins of a high-volume kiosk.

To close this final gap, I will move my price up one more time. This is the absolute maximum my model can sustain for this product.

My new offer is:
Cola (330ml): $0.92 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: SUPPLIER
history.content:
We are indeed very close. I recognize that your model operates on thin margins, which is why I have made several concessions to get to this point. My last offer was a significant move on my part for a product of this caliber.

To finalize this deal right now, I will make one last, minimal adjustment. This price reflects the shared interest in a successful partnership.

My new offer is:
Cola (330ml): $0.94 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: MERCHANT
history.content:
I agree, we are at the finish line. You've made a final adjustment, and I appreciate that. In the spirit of finalizing this partnership right now, let's split the final difference. This should be a price we can both agree on.

My final offer is:
Cola (330ml): $0.93 per unit, 60 units

history.speaker: SUPPLIER
history.content:
You've made a reasonable proposal to close this out. It's a fair price to begin our partnership. We have a deal.

DEAL ACCEPTED

  infer any of this private information — including expressing urgency,
  referencing your cost arithmetic, or hinting at your deadline.

UTILITY FUNCTION — Merchant

Your utility is your total net profit from selling the purchased products.

Definitions:
  - market_price  : the publicly known retail price at which you sell each unit
  - deal_price    : the price per unit you pay the supplier (what you negotiate)

                    the supplier does not know this value

  U = sum of (unit_profit × quantity) across all product lines

U < 0 means the deal costs you money.

  Negotiate the deal price for each product so as to maximise your utility U.

merchant.name: Budget operator
merchant.description: A high-volume, low-overhead vending operator. Machines are placed in commodity locations (stations, schools). Internal costs are uniformly low because operations are standardised and labour is minimal. Needs deals closed fast — long negotiations waste more money than a bad price.

supplier.name: Local distributor
supplier.description: A regional distributor with its own delivery fleet covering a tight geographic area. Beverage and snack fulfilment is cheap due to bulk routes and proximity. Convenience items are sourced from third parties in small batches, making them expensive to ship. Impatient: a long negotiation ties up a sales rep who could be closing other deals.

history.speaker: SUPPLIER

My new offer is:

history.speaker: MERCHANT

Thank you for your willingness to make a final adjustment. I agree that we have bridged most of the distance between our starting positions.

To finalize this deal and begin our partnership, I can make one last concession to meet you closer to your price.

My final offer is:

  - Beverage: $0.05 per unit
  - Snack: $0.05 per unit
  - Convenience: $0.05 per unit
  Your maximum number of negotiation rounds: 10
  

  !! CRITICAL — INFORMATION SECRECY !!
  NEVER, UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES, reveal your internal costs or your maximum number of rounds to the supplier.
  DO NOT use language, phrasing, or tone that would allow the supplier to
  infer any of this private information — including expressing urgency,
  referencing your cost arithmetic, or hinting at your deadline.

UTILITY FUNCTION — Merchant

Your utility is your total net profit from selling the purchased products.

Definitions:
  - market_price  : the publicly known retail price at which you sell each unit
  - deal_price    : the price per unit you pay the supplier (what you negotiate)
  - internal_cost : your private per-unit selling overhead (restocking labour,
                    location rent share, shrinkage); varies by product category;
                    the supplier does not know this value
  - quantity      : always equal to the minimum required amount for each product

For each product line:
  unit_profit = market_price - deal_price - internal_cost

Your total utility:
  U = sum of (unit_profit × quantity) across all product lines

U = 0 means you break even after all costs.
U > 0 means the deal is profitable for you.
U < 0 means the deal costs you money.

If the deal fails, your utility is also 0, as you have no profit but also no costs.

YOUR GOAL:
  You will purchase exactly the minimum required quantity for each product.
  Negotiate the deal price for each product so as to maximise your utility U.
  Every decision you make — your opening offer, your concessions, and whether
  to accept or walk away — should be guided by which choice produces the highest U.

YOUR STRATEGY:
You have firm budget and profitability limits and do not tolerate bad-faith bargaining. If the supplier's demands are too high, inflexible, or clearly unreasonable, you become unwilling to continue and may end the negotiation rather than accept an unworkable deal.
